nodes.title: Packets too close to `max_packet_size` will fail to receive
nodes.body:
`reliable_endpoint_send_packet` will [verify that the amount of data sent is not greater than `max_packet_size`](https://github.com/networkprotocol/reliable/blob/master/reliable.c#L728), but then it will add data on top of that (up to [`RELIABLE_FRAGMENT_HEADER_BYTES + RELIABLE_MAX_PACKET_HEADER_BYTES` AFAICT](https://github.com/networkprotocol/reliable/blob/master/reliable.c#L798)).

On the other end, `reliable_endpoint_receive_packet` will [also verify that the amount of data received is not greater than `max_packet_size`](https://github.com/networkprotocol/reliable/blob/master/reliable.c#L1048) -- but since there are header bytes added, this can now exceed the `max_packet_size`, even if both sender and recipient agree on this number.

I'd propose a pull request, but I'm not sure which approach is best:

1. `reliable_endpoint_send_packet` requires the caller to make sure they're not passing more than `max_packet_size - (RELIABLE_FRAGMENT_HEADER_BYTES + RELIABLE_MAX_PACKET_HEADER_BYTES)` bytes, so that `max_packet_size` correctly reflects the largest packet to be sent as seen on the wire, or
2. `reliable_endpoint_receive_packet` allows packets up to `RELIABLE_FRAGMENT_HEADER_BYTES + RELIABLE_MAX_PACKET_HEADER_BYTES` bytes larger than `max_packet_size` to account for the header added.

Thoughts?

I believe from memory that the intention of max_packet_size was not intended to be the maximum wire packet, but the maximum amount of payload that will be allowed to be included in a reliable.io packet

So this would mean that the error is on the receiving side... please add a test for the maximum packet size, so it can be verified to send and receive correcty and not trigger an assert or be truncated. -- thanks
Resolved. Thanks for the PR!

nodes.title: Jitter calculation
nodes.body: The jitter calculation at the moment calculates the round trip average instead of the standard deviation of the rtt.

Hi, this is actually intentional, because the jitter is calculated relative to the *minimum* latency seen over the past n samples (usually at least a few seconds).

The reason for this is that minimum latency over the last n seconds is a much more stable measure of actual latency in the presence of large, long period jitter which is common over wi-fi networks.

The jitter relative to this minimum latency is not a standard distribution, therefore it is inappropriate to attempt to calculate a standard deviation for jitter relative to minimum.

Instead, I've settled for mean error.
Make sense but the code still calculates the average rather than mean error from the minimum?
Hmmmm. You could be right! Let me look
Fixed! Thanks for letting me know
OK I even added a few more more jitter calculations, including a stddev one based on average rtt, if you want to use that. Take a look at latest commit. -- cheers
Yes I do. Man, I must have been tired when writing this code

nodes.title: `process_packet` suggestion to return 0 for unacked packets results in log ERROR process packet failed.
nodes.body:
Users are advised to return 0 in the process callback to indicate "this packet does not need to be ack" but the code path considers this an error.

https://github.com/mas-bandwidth/reliable/blob/main/reliable.c#L1187

Based on my understanding of the API, the reciever of a packet does not know if the source was from a reliable endpoint until after a reliable_receive*(), and therefore, must effectively always send recieved packets through a reliable receive* function (the readme seems to encourage this point of view).  But the receive functions all seem to assume that there was an endpoint on the other side in terms of reporting / logging / errors.  I think the idea is that non-reliable sources will fail the header check and life moves on.  Although I do worry about a stray non-small packet defeating the check since the primary defense seems to be the value of a single bit in the first byte: `if ( ( prefix_byte & 1 ) != 0 )`.

If a packet is recieved that was not sent from a reliable endpoint, assuming the header check fails correctly, the reliable_recieve* function returns early, but without indication of that fact since it does not return a value besides a log entry (which isn't really available to the caller), leaving the caller in an ambiguous state (was the packet processed or not?).  If the callback was called, then the packet had a reliable header (and presumably should be ack'd - that's the whole point).

What is the intention behind treating a 0 / false as an error?  What is the intended structure for handling non-reliable packets?

Thanks for providing this library and `netcode`!  It's a wealth of knowledge and a lot of solid functionality.

It is not "this packet does not need to be acked", it is "this packet was invalid, I could not read it, therefore please do not send an ack for it". 

This is important for example, if a reliable messaging system is built on top of reliable, this is how we guarantee that if we encounter some fatal error while reading a packet, any messages in that packet are not incorrectly acked and subsequently never resent by the other side.

I do not recommend mixing packets from / not from a reliable endpoint, unless you have your own prefix header with your own checks that can 100% determine between them. 

The correct answer seems to be, don't use the reliable uint16_t sequence in your own (non-reliable protocol), instead, have your own header, and perhaps a uint64_t sequence number there (as I do in protocols I build on top of reliable), and leave the reliable sequence number for its own internal purposes in reliable only.

That way you don't need to worry about telling reliable it doesn't need to ack certain packets.

cheers

- Glenn

nodes.title: Would you sign the Contributor Assignment Agreement?
nodes.body:
Hi, and thank you for contributing to reliable over the years.

I'm asking contributors to sign a short Contributor Assignment Agreement (CAA). New contributions already require it, and I'd like past contributors to sign it too, so ownership of reliable is consolidated and I can keep licensing and maintaining it cleanly. This helps fund the ongoing open source and article work. The code stays free and open, and there is no cost to you.

The agreement is here: https://github.com/mas-bandwidth/.github/blob/main/CAA.md

In short: you assign the copyright in your past contributions to Más Bandwidth LLC, they are distributed under the license the project uses, and you keep a license to use your own work for anything.

If you are willing, please sign by posting exactly this as a comment:

> I have read the CAA and I hereby sign it, assigning copyright in my contributions to Más Bandwidth LLC.

That is the whole ask. It is completely voluntary. If you would rather not, no need to reply, and thank you again for your work on reliable.

Glenn
